summary: AE+SE and Nexus scoped a 2-week POC focused on latency and throughput SLOs. Primary success criteria are clear TTFT vs TPOT targets (p95/p99) per endpoint and an agreed measurement plan with a shared loadgen harness. Baseline runs will establish cold/warm cache behavior; tuned runs will explore batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization variants. Expected next step: share harness, get sample prompts, schedule kickoff.
topics: Benchmark methodology: loadgen, cold vs warm, priming
transcript:
[00:00] Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-30
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Samira Khan (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Evan Park (Redwood SE), Alex Morgan (Nexus CTO), Priya Shah (Nexus ML), Mateo Rivera (Nexus Infra), Joon Kim (Nexus PM)

[00:12] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — align on success criteria for the POC, workload sizing, what we measure (TTFT vs TPOT), and the measurement plan + timeline.

[00:30] Alex: Sounds good. We're mostly worried about latency for our chat flow; we need consistent p95 for first reply and also overall token throughput.

[00:45] Jordan: Great. Quick definitions to make sure we're aligned: TTFT — time to first token, i.e. time from request accept to the first byte. TPOT — time per output token, average or percentile of per-token generation. We'll capture both p95 and p99 for each.

[01:20] Priya: Ok, so what numbers should we aim for? We have an internal goal of p95 TTFT < 200ms for our main 1k-concurrent user flow and p99 < 400ms. For per-token we were thinking p95 ~ 30ms/token, p99 ~ 60ms/token. Those are rough.

[01:50] Jordan: Those are reasonable as starting targets. For context, on Dedicated GPU pools we typically see TTFT in the 50-300ms range depending on model and KV cache hit rate, and TPOT depends a lot on quantization and batching. We should separate out cold TTFT (cold model load / cold KV) vs warm TTFT.

[02:20] Mateo: For infra constraints: we can provision Dedicated capacity for the POC, or we can run on Redwood Hosted. We prefer Dedicated if it helps hit targets, but cost is a factor.

[02:35] Evan: Noted. For the measurement plan we recommend:
- baseline runs (no priming cache, measure cold/warm)
- steady-state runs with realistic token-length distribution
- ramp tests for concurrency to find bottlenecks
- p95/p99 extraction and breakdowns (network, queuing, model compute).

[03:10] Joon: Can you elaborate on dataset and prompts? We have a mix: 60% short queries (~10-25 tokens), 30% medium (50-120), 10% long (200-600).

[03:30] Priya: Yep that's our distribution, and we also have some multi-turn contexts that rely on KV cache to avoid re-decoding prefixes.

[03:45] Jordan: Perfect — that token distribution matters a lot. For KV / prefix caching impact we'll do two passes: primed (simulate warm KV hits) and unprimed (cold). That will show delta in TTFT and overall tokens/sec.

[04:15] Alex: We heard about TTFT vs TPOT confusion internally. Can you give a simple rule of thumb for how to value them?

[04:30] Samira: Sure — TTFT maps closely to user perceived latency for first response (critical for chat UX), whereas TPOT affects streaming smoothness and throughput at scale. If you need snappy first responses, optimize TTFT. If you need high aggregate throughput, optimize TPOT and batching. Both matter; POC will measure both.

[05:05] Mateo: Any guidance on p95 vs p99? Our product SLOs are pretty strict at p99.

[05:20] Jordan: We recommend targeting p95 targets first, then measure p99 and look for outliers. P99 often exposes tail that is network or cold-start related; we should capture traces to attribute tails to model cold, queuing, or infra jitter.

[05:50] Priya: For the POC success criteria we propose:
- TTFT p95 < 200ms, TTFT p99 < 450ms (warm);
- TPOT p95 < 35ms/token, TPOT p99 < 70ms/token;
- 95% of requests served without falling back to smaller model;
- Throughput: sustain X tokens/sec target for our expected concurrency (we'll provide concurrency target).

[06:30] Jordan: We'll validate those; we typically ask for a concrete concurrency target — e.g., 500 concurrent connections with the token distribution you provided. That maps to an expected tokens/sec which we will provision against.

[07:00] Alex: Let's start with a baseline concurrency of 300 and a ramp to 1000 for stress. We'll share weekly average and peak numbers.

[07:18] Evan: Good. Measurement plan details: we'll use the Redwood loadgen harness (link will be provided) which supports priming, concurrency ramps, and exports p95/p99 plus breakdown CSVs. We'll run baseline on Hosted and then on Dedicated with default batching and then with tuned batching/quantization.

[07:50] Mateo: For Dedicated, what hardware profiles do you typically recommend? A100 80GB or H100 nodes?

[08:05] Jordan: For high throughput and low TPOT, H100s are best but more expensive; A100S can be fine depending on model. For the first pass we'll do a medium-size model on A100 equivalent, then if needed try H100. We'll include kernel/compilation notes in the report.

[08:40] Priya: How long will each benchmark run take? We want stable measurements.

[08:50] Evan: Baseline runs: 30 minutes for warm steady-state per config (after priming), ramp tests ~15-20 minutes, cold-start tests include model load cycles and can take longer. For POC we plan 2 baseline days: day 1 baseline + tuning, day 2 final confirmation; overall 2 weeks to cycle through variants and provide a report.

[09:25] Joon: Timeline sounds fine. What artifacts will we get?

[09:30] Samira: We'll deliver raw CSVs, summary report with p95/p99 tables, latency breakdown (network/queuing/compute), recommended config (batching size, KV policy, quantization), and cost estimates for production scaling.

[09:55] Alex: Good. A few clarifying questions: 1) Will you simulate our real user distribution (multi-turn sessions)? 2) How do you account for KV cache hit rates?

[10:10] Jordan: Yes to both — the harness can replay multi-turn sessions with context length and will simulate KV hit rates by pre-priming a % of traffic. We'll run a series: 0% primed, 50% primed, 90% primed to show delta.

[10:32] Priya: Are you measuring end-to-end TTFT including network ingress/egress, or just the model time?

[10:40] Evan: We'll measure both: synthetic client-side TTFT (end-to-end) and the service-side breakdown using tracing. We'll correlate them to show where tails come from.

[11:00] Mateo: For private deployments we have to go through security checks. Will you provide audit logs and SOC2 docs?

[11:10] Samira: Yes — we'll share our SOC 2, ISO references, and logging details. We'll include a doc link in the follow-up.

[11:25] Alex: Ok, what about model variants? We might try a 30B open model and a 7B lower-latency model as fallback.

[11:36] Jordan: Perfect — we'll run both. We'll include automatic fallback measurement (how often requests fall back to the smaller model under load). That ties to your success criteria of <5% fallback.

[12:05] Priya: Any gotchas around quantization and accuracy regressions? We need to keep response quality near baseline.

[12:18] Evan: We'll include quality checks using a small eval set (50-100 prompts) and quality thresholds (agreement / Rouge / similarity) before applying aggressive quantization. If regression exceeds agreed threshold we'll flag it.

[12:50] Alex: OK good. Let's talk numbers again — for the POC report we want a clear table: config, TTFT p95/p99, TPOT p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost estimate.

[13:10] Samira: Yep that's the standard output. We'll also include jitter plots and tail attribution.

[13:30] Joon: Any network peering requirements for private?

[13:38] Mateo: We can open a test VPC peering and sample credentials; we just need the requirements documented.

[13:44] Samira: We'll send a checklist for VPC peering + firewall rules in the follow-up.

[14:00] Priya: For success criteria sign-off — who from Nexus will sign off?

[14:08] Alex: I'll own the sign-off for technical success, Joon will own product acceptance.

[14:15] Samira: Great. Quick recap of next steps: Samira/Jordan to share harness, infra templates, and SOC docs; Nexus to share prompts and open peering if Private; schedule kickoff week of 2027-10-04. POC timeline: 2 weeks of runs with interim demo at end of week 1 and final report at end of week 2.

[14:42] Alex: Sounds good. Anything else?

[14:47] Priya: One more nit: please include how you measure p99 when traffic is low — sampling can be noisy.

[14:55] Jordan: We'll bootstrap with longer runs and aggregate across windows; we'll also provide confidence intervals and note when sample size is small.

[15:10] Samira: Alright thanks everyone. We'll put the next steps in email and Slack.

[15:20] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional fillers and overlaps. Some product names transcribed slightly differently (e.g., "KV cache" typed as "K-V cash" in an auto-gen line).
